claims.text: NbTaTiV is a refractory BCC high-entropy alloy that remains single-phase BCC up to approximately 900°C.
NbTaTiV exhibits severe lattice distortion because of large atomic-size mismatches and compositional fluctuations.
Random multi-principal-element mixing with substantial atomic-size mismatch produces high lattice distortion.
Selecting elements with similar atomic radii or inducing partial ordering reduces lattice distortion and local compositional fluctuations.
NbTaTiV has been tested by in situ neutron diffraction and compression at room temperature, 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C at a strain rate of 1 × 10^-4 s^-1.
At temperatures up to about 900°C and a strain rate near 10^-4 s^-1, thermally activated dislocation processes are prominent.
Severe lattice distortion causes edge dislocations to adopt wavy, non-planar line configurations.
Lattice distortion forces dislocation cores to deviate from their neutral planes.
Pronounced lattice distortion disrupts the ideal dislocation-core structure.
Lattice distortion favors activation and glide of <111>{110} edge dislocations over screw dislocations.
Wavy edge-dislocation configurations have lower high-temperature mobility barriers.
Screw-dislocation-controlled deformation generally limits ductility in conventional BCC metals.
Lower barriers for edge-dislocation motion permit easier dislocation transmission and reduce stress localization.
A transition toward edge-dislocation-mediated glide increases high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
Relative to a low-distortion control, the high-distortion alloy should exhibit more edge-dislocation activity and wavier dislocation lines.
Relative to a low-distortion control, the high-distortion alloy should have greater elevated-temperature ductility and toughness.
A reduced-distortion refractory BCC control would rely more strongly on screw-dislocation activity and exhibit lower high-temperature plasticity.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only when lattice distortion dominates the response and may fail in other crystal structures or when precipitation strengthening dominates.
Dynamic recovery or precipitation effects may alter the response over extended temperature ranges or at different strain rates.
